blocks.title: Plenary Discussion I: State of coffee production and consumption in Southeast Asia and China (China/Vietnam/Thai/Indonesia)
blocks.about: Coffee was introduced into these four countries at different periods and for different purposes, and the resulting landscapes differ accordingly: an established export industry in Vietnam, a plateau economy originating in colonial plantations in Laos, a state-supported highland development crop in Thailand, and a rapid shift from bulk supply to specialty production in Yunnan. All four now face a period in which open trade cannot be assumed and domestic consumption is growing quickly. This plenary brings together perspectives from research, trade and roasting to review the current situation in each country, and to consider what would be required for the region to trade more directly within itself.

papers.title: A Transient Coffee Landscape: Crisis, Trial, and the Restructuring of Chinese Capital in Late 19th-Century Malacca
papers.abstract:
In the late nineteenth century, the agricultural landscape of Malacca underwent a dramatic transformation due to the rapid decline of the traditional tapioca industry. Facing exhausted land and labor shortages, local Chinese capitalists initiated a pragmatic transition that briefly reshaped the region into a promising coffee landscape. Utilizing historical newspapers, colonial agricultural show records, and Kew Gardens correspondence, this paper examines the experimental cultivation of Liberian coffee in Malacca.
Although Malaccan Liberian coffee received exceptional evaluations from London brokers within the imperial botanical network, it failed to establish a permanent plantation landscape. High post-harvest processing thresholds, significant financial deficits, and a depressed global coffee market prevented widespread cultivation. However, this transient coffee landscape was not a dead end but a vital spatial and economic bridge. The physical infrastructure (such as converted tapioca factories), labor networks, and institutional experiences accumulated by Chinese planters during this coffee experiment facilitated a swift pivot to emerging cash crops like tea and rubber. Ultimately, this ephemeral coffee landscape laid the critical physical and commercial foundation for Malaya's twentieth-century rubber boom.
papers.keywords: Malacca · Chinese Capital · Liberian Coffee · Plantation Economy

papers.title: "Two Days Won't Do": A Told Landscape of Yunnan Coffee A Work-in-Progress Oral History and Visual Ethnography
papers.affiliation: Lecturer of Sociology in School of Ethnology and Sociology, Yunnan University
papers.abstract:
At the northern edge of the Southeast Asian upland coffee belt, Xiaowaozi Coffee Estate in Pu'er, Yunnan, shows how a coffee landscape is narrated and remembered. This paper presents a work-in-progress oral history and ethnographic film project based on ten days of fieldwork in August 2025 with the estate's founder, Mr. Liao.
Born in Hainan, where coffee was introduced by returned overseas Chinese from Southeast Asia, Mr. Liao was trained at the South China Institute of Tropical Agriculture and state-assigned to Yunnan. He worked tropical crops in Xishuangbanna before Nestlé's arrival brought him to Pu'er; after retirement, he bought a hillside hollow and became a roaster, café owner, and host. One life thus crosses three regimes—state assignment, contract farming, and family estate branding—condensing four decades of the region's coffee history.
The project's core observation is the told landscape: after decades of media coverage, Mr. Liao delivers a polished, pamphlet-like account with remarkable consistency. Through the slow presence he demands (“People come for two days and want to write about me; rushing through won't work”), the project traces how this public narrative yields to the personal—the technician's account, and finally the Hainanese layer: private memories of the homeland and family he left. On camera he rarely faces the lens; he addresses his photo albums. The estate emerges from what he looks at as much as from what he says.

papers.title: Paksong’s Coffee, Colonial Legacy to Indigenous Identity
papers.affiliation: World Wild Fund for Nature Laos (WWF-Laos)
papers.abstract:
Coffee arrived in many highland regions not as a gift but as an order. French colonial administrations in the early-to-mid 20th century saw the cool, high-altitude built on ancient volcanic terrain long inhabited by indigenous hill tribes and recognized only ideal terroir for a lucrative export crop. Plantations were carved from ancestral land through seizure and coercive policy, leaving local communities little say over their own ground.

Independence did not return land overnight, but it opened a door. Plantation structures fragmented over subsequent decades, and smallholder plots replaced centralized colonial estates. Indigenous families began working the same slopes their grandparents had once farmed under orders not fully or cleanly, given land disputes and market structures still favoring large exporters, but the direction was unmistakable from labor to stewardship.

What elevates this beyond economics is what happened to coffee’s meaning. For many hill tribe communities, it stopped being a foreign imposition and became a livelihood woven into cultural identity household processing techniques, village varietals, generational knowledge as pride rather than instruction. Cooperatives formed by indigenous growers began controlling not just farming but the story of the coffee itself, letting a family’s heritage travel from beans to cups worldwide a reversal of the crop’s anonymous, extractive origins.

The deepest shift is in the relationship to land. Where colonial farming prioritized short-term extraction, many growers now combine inherited ecological knowledge intercropping, shade management, water stewardship with coffee’s demands, treating the land as multigenerational responsibility rather than a resource to exhaust.

Coffee’s journey through these highlands mirrors colonial extraction giving way to self-determination a crop born of forced labor now representing continuity, independence, attraction for ecotourism and a family’s claim to the mountain they have always called home.
papers.keywords: Paksong · Indigenous · Coffee · Colonial

papers.title: The history of coffee, coffee-drinking culture, and social life in Aceh through Malay manuscript sources
papers.abstract: A cup of Acehnese coffee carries questions of history, sociability, and cultural knowledge that this study proposes to investigate through manuscripts. The study approaches coffee as a subject through which to explore the relationships between everyday consumption, social interaction, and the transmission of cultural knowledge. The study will use philological reading and historical contextualisation to examine Hikayat Gomtala Syah, Hikayat Kureh Pari, Tajul Muluk, and Hikayat Aceh for references to coffee and its consumption, with attention to textual provenance, dating, genre, and the circumstances in which particular accounts were produced. It asks how coffee and its consumption are represented in these sources, what social settings and relationships become visible through those representations, and how manuscript evidence can inform an understanding of Aceh’s living coffee culture. Particular attention will be given to the evidential limits of the sources and to the distinction between historical documentation and present-day interpretations of coffee traditions. The study will consider how locally situated accounts from Aceh can contribute to wider discussions of coffee as a commodity, a cultural practice, and a medium of knowledge exchange within Southeast Asia. Its intended contribution is to bring manuscript evidence into dialogue with the study of everyday social life and material culture, while identifying questions of continuity and change that require further investigation. The presentation will also incorporate selected Acehnese coffee samples and a traditional coffee cup as interpretive materials to support discussion of the relationships between written accounts, material objects, and contemporary coffee-drinking practices.
papers.keywords: Aceh · coffee history · manuscripts · coffee-drinking culture · social life

papers.title: Tasting the tradition: Coffee, Coorg, and the narratives of the ‘native’
papers.affiliation: Department of Sociology, School of Humanities and Social Sciences, Shiv Nadar Institute of Eminence, Deemed to be University, Delhi NCR
papers.abstract:
This paper explores how third-wave coffee makers, together with a set of partnering growers, reclaim the legacy of native culture by creating an affective economy centered on the sensorial characteristics of Coffee grown in native habitats. Since India’s coffee sector entered the free market in the mid-1990s, coffee has circulated through an expanding network of trading units, curing mills, and auction centers, transforming its movement and valuation. Based on my fieldwork across these institutions in the plantation villages of Coorg in Karnataka, South India, this paper articulates how coffee is represented and valued for its flavor and aroma, which simultaneously corresponds to the ways in which it is grown and cared for. 
Following global trends towards specialty and artisanal coffee, a few Kodavas, the local dominant community, have recently begun marketing their coffee as grown in ecologically diverse native habitats that produce premium-quality cups. This emerging value regime privileges flavor and aroma over conventional commercial coffee metrics such as size, color, moisture, and gravity. Growers, roasters, and Q-graders from Coorg work together to present ‘Coorg Coffee’ as a distinct sensorial object that both reflects its taste properties and represents the ‘native eco-system’ as the material condition in which coffee grows and develops its flavor profile. This native ecology is demonstrated as the reflection of Kodava cosmology, characterized by love for the land, preservation of tradition, and sacred forests, which becomes integral to coffee’s sensory value. 
Following anthropological literature on the production of quality in plantation economies (Besky 2020, Fischer 2022), this paper demonstrates that taste is coproduced through material, social, and discursive relations. Specialty coffee market, I argue, functions through an affective network among the grower, the coffee, and the consumer, navigated by the stories of Kodava life forms and the sustainable farming embedded in them.
papers.keywords: India · Specialty Coffee · Tradition · Native ecology

papers.title: Daytime Parties in the Name of Coffee: Reconfiguring Spaces of Consumption and Sociality in Thailand
papers.affiliation: Graduate School of Asian and African Area Studies, Kyoto University
papers.abstract:
Research on Thai coffee culture has examined cultural hybridity and the symbolic value of consumption associated with café images. Studies of café sociality have also highlighted how operators and customers shape spaces for interaction. Building on these insights, this paper examines “coffee raves,” daytime events combining coffee, music, and dancing. It asks how these events are organized in different commercial settings and what meanings and roles are assigned to coffee in the process.
The paper draws primarily on participant observation, conversations with attendees, and an interview at a café in Chiang Mai. An interview with a bar operator in Bangkok provides contrasting material on event planning and operation. In Chiang Mai, furniture in a café ordinarily used for working and spending time is rearranged to accommodate dancing. Attendees arrive through friends’ invitations and social media, and observations document moments of joining others in dancing. In Bangkok, an initiative framed as a healthy daytime party also sought to attract new customers. The operator described adding alcohol and food to accommodate preferences and longer visits, while recruiting attendees through DJs and running clubs.
These materials suggest the limits of explaining coffee raves solely through shared interests in coffee or health. At the café, dancing is incorporated into an everyday setting for spending time; at the bar, coffee is invoked as a reason for partying earlier in the day. Their realization involves practical adjustments to networks, refreshments, and space. By situating coffee’s cultural meanings within the practices of attracting people and organizing places to spend time together, this paper examines the social spaces of coffee consumption in urban Thailand.
papers.keywords: Coffee culture · Chiang Mai · cafés · sociality · coffee consumption

papers.title: Beyond the Instant Packet: Coffee Mix and Collective Deliberation in Karen Agrarian Landscapes
papers.abstract: In the forested agrarian landscapes of Southeast Myanmar, Indigenous Karen  communities maintain customary land governance (Kaw) and agroforestry livelihoods deeply intertwined with local natural resources. Yet, an intriguing cultural and material paradox exists across rural non-coffee-producing villages in this region: despite the absence of coffee bean farming, processing, or commercial teashop (laphet tye saing) culture, pre-packaged, industrial "3-in-1" coffee mix has become an indispensable technology of political and social life. Drawing on qualitative ethnographic fieldwork conducted between December 1 and December 17, 2025—comprising 24 semi-structured interviews and participant observations across village clusters—this study investigates the material, sensory, spatial, and gendered dimensions of instant coffee mix consumption. The findings reveal that coffee mix is deliberately withheld from daily routine labor and reserved exclusively as an "extraordinary" commodity for moments of formal assembly, guest reception, and community advancement meetings. Reaching for a factory-sealed sachet acts as a material boundary marker, re-spatializing the private domestic veranda (hter) into an autonomous political forum. The sensory properties of the beverage—its distinct aroma, concentrated sweetness, and rapid solubility—establish an affective social contract that fosters bodily alertness, calms interpersonal tension, and structures the temporal rhythms of consensus-building around land tenure and local security. Crucially, this public sphere of deliberation is underwritten by women’s affective and domestic labor, as women manage commodity reserves, control procurement, and prepare the beverage, serving as vital gatekeepers of local political space. By bridging political ecology, sensory anthropology, and material culture, this paper challenges production-centric biases in coffee geography. It demonstrates that agricultural commodities must be understood beyond zones of extraction, highlighting how Indigenous communities in conflict-affected borderlands strategically appropriate mass-manufactured consumer goods to sustain autonomous governance, collective solidarity, and political sovereignty.
papers.keywords: Coffee Mix · Karen Communities · Political Assembly

papers.title: An Anthropological Perspective on Vietnamese Coffee Culture
papers.affiliation: Researcher, Vietnam National Institute of Culture and Arts, Vietnam
papers.abstract:
Vietnam is not only famous for its rice cultivation, but is also one of the world's largest rice exporters. Its vast rice paddies stretch from north to south, and rice farming has become an important part of Vietnam's economic development. Father Alexander Vallet, a French priest, introduced the first coffee trees to Vietnam. However, the region's ecological environment and geographical conditions were unsuitable for coffee cultivation, so the coffee industry did not develop.

From 1925 to 1945, Vietnam gradually became a famous coffee-producing region. Due to its geographical location and climate, coffee is not only a popular beverage among Vietnamese people, but also a daily leisure activity and a cultural expression, a characteristic of Vietnamese culture. Whether enjoying a cup of fragrant hot coffee on a cold morning in Hanoi or sitting with friends on a rainy afternoon in Saigon, this has become a habit for many Vietnamese, forming a local cultural feature. What are the differences between the coffee cultures of Saigon and Hanoi? Hanoi and Saigon are the two largest cities in Vietnam and the centers of Vietnam's economic, political, cultural development and international exchange. The two cities, located approximately 1,730 kilometers apart, possess unique cultural characteristics, one of which is their coffee culture. Comparing the development of coffee consumption in Hanoi and Saigon, we can see significant differences in their social backgrounds and socio-ecological environments, resulting in their respective unique coffee cultures. Let's examine the following differences:

1. Coffee brewing methods, unique coffee flavors, and different names.

2. Places for enjoying coffee: at home, street-side coffee shops, large-scale coffee shops, and coffee chain stores.

3. Coffee drinkers: factors such as gender, age, and occupation all influence individual coffee drinking habits.

Through the above points, the author hopes to introduce Vietnamese coffee culture for discussion and academic exchange at the conference.

papers.title: Designing Coffee Tourism: “Autonomous Design” and Indigenous Entrepreneurship in a Karen Community in Northern Thailand
papers.affiliation: Department of Tourism and Transnational Studies
papers.abstract:
Coffee has traditionally been regarded as a commodity that epitomizes the “North–South divide.” Specifically, critics have pointed to an unequal structure in which producers in the “South” (the Global South) grow coffee to meet demand in the “North” (developed nations), while the North dominates global coffee markets and captures the majority of the profits. In recent years, however, as coffee markets and cultures have matured, new initiatives have emerged in some producing regions that seek to independently manage the entire process, from cultivation and roasting to marketing and sales. Through this process of “sixth-sector industrialization” in coffee production, some coffee-related activities have also developed into new forms of “coffee tourism” by forging connections with the tourism sector.

   This presentation examines emerging trends in coffee tourism, focusing on Northern Thailand, where coffee markets and coffee culture have expanded rapidly since the 2010s. In ethnic Karen villages in Mae Hong Son Province, where the author has conducted fieldwork since the early 2000s, a recent phenomenon has emerged in which young people who previously worked in urban areas are returning to their home villages. These returnees are attempting to create autonomous spaces by combining traditional ways of life with the knowledge and experience they have acquired through urban life. As a case study, this presentation examines a coffee cultivation project launched by these returnees in 2023 through the perspectives of “autonomous design” (Escobar 2018) and “Indigenous entrepreneurship” (Eijdenberg et al. 2025), and explores its potential to foster alternative forms of economic and social development.
papers.keywords: coffee tourism · the Karen · Thailand · “autonomous design” · Indigenous entrepreneurship

papers.title: Brewing Mental Wellness: Craft Coffee Tourism as a Healing Experience, Ethical Commodification, and Destination Governance Opportunity in Vietnam
papers.abstract: Historically, health and wellness tourism has been dominated by spas and clinical settings, yet emerging evidence suggests that craft-based food tourism may offer meaningful mental wellness outcomes outside conventional therapeutic contexts. This case study examines how a Vietnamese coffee brand leverages farm-to-cup tourism to foster mindfulness, sensory awareness, and intellectual wellbeing among visitors. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with the founder and participant observation at the farm's roastery and café, the study explores the intersection of food tourism and individual wellbeing. Findings reveal that the multisensory experience of observing coffee beans, engaging with varying roasting profiles, and participating in cupping (tasting) rituals cultivates a mindfulness practice of slowing down and sensory attunement. This experience counteracts the negative effects of consumerism on tourists' intellectual wellbeing by fostering pride and knowledge of product provenance, while also serving as a partial healing mechanism outside clinical settings (Zheng et al., 2025). From a supply-side perspective, the case highlights significant governance challenges, including the owner's commitment to maintaining a quality, authentic, non-scaled product at the expense of digital marketing, and the absence of state acknowledgment of "wellness food tourism." These dynamics illuminate broader issues of inequality and care commodification: while wealthy international tourists constitute the target market, local community members and poorer travelers are largely excluded. Moreover, local tourism boards lack the coordination necessary to integrate wellness tourism and craft producers into broader destination strategies. The study concludes by offering governance recommendations for destination managers to develop "wellness routes"—networks connecting diverse producers to different traveler segments—to ensure that the mental health benefits of craft tourism are sustained and equitably distributed. This case contributes to emerging discourse on alternative wellness tourism models and their potential for inclusive, community-oriented mental health promotion.
papers.keywords: wellness tourism · food tourism · mental health · Vietnam · craft coffee · governance · mindfulness

papers.title: From Coffee Production to Experiential Landscapes: Resource Orchestration and Value Co-creation in Baoshan and Pu’er, Yunnan
papers.abstract: Coffee tourism is increasingly used by producing regions to connect agricultural production with visitor experience, cultural communication, and rural economic diversification. Existing studies have highlighted its contributions to visitor experience, destination branding, stakeholder cooperation, and sustainability. Much of this work, however, examines tourism outcomes or destination-level development, paying less attention to how coffee-producing enterprises organize place-specific resources and convert production and sensory knowledge into experiential and market value. This study addresses this process through an embedded comparative case study of Gongjiang Coffee Estate in Baoshan and Dakaihe Coffee Estate in Pu'er, Yunnan Province, China. It draws on field observations, preliminary interviews, and estate documents and promotional materials. Integrating resource orchestration, experiential value co-creation, and place branding, the study examines how production, ecological, cultural, and knowledge resources are selected, combined, and presented to visitors. Preliminary analysis suggests that both estates create value not simply by adding tourism services to coffee production, but by reorganizing production spaces, place narratives, and coffee knowledge into coherent visitor experiences. Gongjiang places relatively greater emphasis on production visibility and participatory “seed-to-cup” activities, which connect process knowledge with perceptions of authenticity, quality, and brand trust. Dakaihe draws more strongly on ecological cultivation, biodiversity, origin narratives, and sensory learning to reinforce place identity and the value of specialty coffee. The comparison also foregrounds the need to distinguish commercial value creation from the distribution of benefits among enterprises, farmers, and local communities. The study develops a management-oriented explanation of coffee landscape transformation and offers practical implications for coffee enterprises and producing regions in Southeast Asia seeking locally embedded pathways beyond raw-bean production.
papers.keywords: coffee tourism · agritourism · experiential value · knowledge mediation · place branding · comparative case study

papers.title: Body, Nature, and the Gaze: A Study on the Cheat code forviews and Cultural Mechanisms of China's influencer Cafes
papers.affiliation: School of Law and Politics, Yunnan University of Finance and Economics
papers.abstract:
In recent years, various influencer Cafés that combine sensory experiences such as taste and sight have emerged in China, becoming a new form of tourism in the context of cultural and tourism integration. This study focuses on several
popular and highly representative influencer Cafes in China, conducting an in-depth analysis to argue that visiting these cafés has become a cultural phenomenon reflecting nature, visual aesthetics, and bodily experience within tourism. Judging from
current forms—such as waterfall cafés and cave cafés—coffee consumption is deeply integrated with tourism experiences, involving observation, physical sensations, and people's exploration and aspirations toward nature. In today’s tourism consumption, gaze theory and embodiment theory alone are insufficient to fully explain the underlying cultural and social meanings and the mechanisms behind this phenomenon. Drawing on cultural sociology, this study attempts to analyze the cultural mechanisms emerging from the fusion of symbolic consumption and bodily experience, thereby proposing a new theoretical framework for understanding tourism experiences.

papers.title: INVENTING COFFEE CULTURE: SOCIAL SPACES, CONSUMPTION PRACTICES, AND ETHNIC IDENTITY AMONG THE Ê ĐÊ OF ĐẮK LẮK, VIETNAM
papers.abstract:
INVENTING COFFEE CULTURE: SOCIAL SPACES, CONSUMPTION PRACTICES, AND ETHNIC IDENTITY AMONG THE Ê ĐÊ OF ĐẮK LẮK, VIETNAM
Ly.D.T 
Abstract
Vietnam is one of the world’s major coffee-producing countries, yet discussions of coffee have largely emphasized its economic significance as a global commodity, with less attention to the local and Indigenous cultural processes through which coffee is appropriated and transformed. This paper examines the “invention of coffee culture” among the Ê Đê of Đắk Lắk, Vietnam, a major coffee-producing region.
Drawing on more than three years of ethnographic fieldwork, including participant observation and approximately 15–20 in-depth interviews in Buôn Ma Thuột, Krông Ana, and Krông Pắc, the paper examines how coffee has been incorporated, reinterpreted, and localized within Ê Đê social and cultural life. It focuses on the emergence of new social spaces and everyday consumption practices; and the production and negotiation of Ê Đê cultural identity through coffee.
Drawing on the concepts of “invented tradition” and cultural production, the paper argues that Ê Đê coffee culture is neither a simple adoption of an external commodity nor a straightforward continuation of an inherited tradition. Rather, it emerges through selective processes of cultural adaptation and reconfiguration, in which traditional communal values, cultural memories, ethnic identity, and contemporary market and tourism demands are continually negotiated.
The paper contributes to broader discussions of coffee culture in Southeast Asia by demonstrating how a global commodity becomes localized through Indigenous cultural practices while simultaneously reshaping social spaces, cultural meanings, and ethnic representation.
papers.keywords: Ê Đê · coffee culture · social space · consumption practices · cultural production · invented tradition · Đắk Lắk · Vietnam

papers.title: From Ritual Hospitality to Digital Distinction: Revaluing Coffee in Urban Indonesia
papers.abstract:
**From Ritual Hospitality to Digital Distinction: Revaluing Coffee in Urban Indonesia**

Coffee in Indonesia is commonly described either as an agricultural commodity or as a rapidly expanding urban lifestyle. This paper argues that its contemporary social significance is better understood as a process of **revaluation**, through which inherited meanings of hospitality, ritual, locality, and sociality are selectively translated into new forms of commercial, symbolic, and digital value. Drawing on qualitative field research in Jakarta, Yogyakarta, and Makassar, including observations in traditional and modern coffee spaces and semi-structured interviews with fifteen consumers and five coffee-industry practitioners, the study compares how coffee acquires different meanings across three urban contexts.

The findings identify four interrelated modes of social valuation: religious and ritual hospitality, social relationship, life-cycle commemoration, and social distinction. In Makassar, coffee remains embedded in post-Ramadan religious gatherings while regional origins such as Toraja and Kalosi are simultaneously reformulated as markers of authenticity and local identity in modern cafés. In Yogyakarta, vernacular coffee practices coexist with specialty cafés, coffee catering, and creative communities, while in Jakarta coffee shops increasingly operate as spaces of professional networking, lifestyle performance, and status differentiation. Across the three cities, cafés, branding practices, origin narratives, visual aesthetics, and social media transform coffee from a beverage into a medium for constructing identity and distinction.

Rather than representing a linear shift from tradition to modernity, these processes demonstrate how local meanings are repeatedly reworked through commodity circulation and digital representation. The paper proposes the notion of **urban coffee landscapes as infrastructures of valuation**, where place, ritual, taste, class, and mediated visibility intersect. It contributes to understanding how Southeast Asian coffee cultures are being transformed not through the disappearance of local traditions, but through their selective incorporation into contemporary markets and regimes of distinction.
papers.keywords: Keywords: coffee landscape · social valuation · urban coffee culture · distinction · commodity · Indonesia

papers.title: The Changing Trajectory of Community-Based Coffee Farming and Processing in Barangay Talbak, Doña Remedios Trinidad, Bulacan, Philippines
papers.abstract: This study explores the evolving landscape of community-based coffee farming and processing in Barangay Talbak, located in Doña Remedios Trinidad, Bulacan, Philippines. The history of coffee farming in this community is linked to the migration of families from Cavite, a region in the southern Philippines, during the 1960s and 1970s. These settlers moved to Talbak in search of agricultural land and brought with them the knowledge and practices associated with coffee cultivation. Over time, coffee farming has become an integral part of the community's agricultural livelihood and local knowledge. This qualitative study aims to understand how the coffee landscape has evolved by examining the experiences and perspectives of coffee farmers and other key community members. Using a historical-contextual approach, the study will conduct semi-structured interviews to explore the development of coffee farming and processing. It will investigate the factors that have influenced its changing trajectory, as well as the responses and adaptations of local farmers. The interviews will be analyzed thematically to identify patterns related to production, processing, livelihoods, markets, environmental conditions, agricultural knowledge, and other factors shaping the community’s coffee landscape. By documenting the experiences and perspectives of coffee-growing communities in Talbak, this study offers a localized perspective on broader discussions of coffee landscapes in Southeast Asia. It specifically addresses issues of migration, knowledge, livelihoods, and the evolving nature of community-based coffee production.
papers.keywords: coffee farming · coffee landscapes · coffee processing · migration · community-based agriculture

papers.title: Bean Sourcing, Taking Root, and Co-building: The Practices and Contributions of "New Yunnanese" in Menglian's Coffee Industry from a Broker Perspective
papers.affiliation: Professor of Sociology, School of Ethnology and Sociology, Yunnan University, Doctoral Student of Sociology, School of Ethnology and Sociology, Yunnan University
papers.abstract:
Located along the China–Myanmar border, Menglian County in Yunnan Province has, in recent years, emerged as a new space for talent agglomeration and local innovation, driven by the development of the specialty coffee industry and the rise of the lifestyle migration economy. Taking the case of a Shanghai-based coffee bean sourcer who settled in Menglian and became actively involved in building a digital nomad community,
this study adopts a broker perspective to examine how "New Yunnanese" achieve local embeddedness through participation in the coffee industry, and to analyze their practices and contributions to local development. The findings show that "New Yunnanese" are not merely participants in the coffee industry; they also serve as key brokers connecting local governments, industry stakeholders, coffee farmers, and newly mobile populations. By integrating resources, building social relationships, and facilitating cross-regional networks, they promote the dissemination of specialty coffee culture, the development of digital nomad communities, and the construction of local brands, thereby fostering the collaborative development of industry, community, and place. The Menglian case further demonstrates that the significance of "New Yunnanese" lies not simply in relocating to a new locality, but in continuously activating local development through cross-boundary connections. This study provides a new sociological perspective on the social mechanisms through which specialty industries contribute to the development of border counties.
papers.keywords: Specialty Coffee Industry · New Yunnanese · Broker · Local Embeddedness · Collaborative Place-making

papers.title: Beyond Evasion: Coffee, Agrarian Capitalism, and State Engagement in an Akha Community of Northern Thailand
papers.affiliation: Faculty of Social Sciences, Chiang Mai University
papers.abstract:
This research explores the agrarian transition and capitalization process within Mae Chan Tai, an Akha ethnic village in northern Thailand, following the introduction of commercial coffee farming. The study aims to address the central research question "How does integration into capitalism change the relationships of an ethnic community with the state and among its members ?" To answer this, the research expands upon James C. Scott’s concept of Zomia by employing Tania Murray Li’s concepts of Governmentality and Rendering Technical, alongside Henry Bernstein’s Agrarian Differentiation Theory. Data were collected using a qualitative approach comprising in-depth interviews and field observations.
The findings reveal three significant shifts. First, through agricultural commercialization supported by the Royal Project and the organization such as GIAPSA (NPO), the villagers have transitioned from evading state authority to actively interacting with the state and global markets, using coffee as an economic intermediary. Second, this transition to capitalism has transformed the villagers' social identities from collective agricultural laborers to competitive business entrepreneurs. This leads to a process of social differentiation affecting agrarian relationships, reflected by the emergence of 15 coffee brands among only 43 households, thereby drawing a line that turns traditional interdependent relationships into market competition. Finally, the economic success of the local coffee industry has attracted the younger generation back to the village, running counter to the common trend of rural-to-urban migration. This economic strength not only rebuilds the community's demographic future but may also open up space for studying bargaining power with the state in other dimensions. This study demonstrates that the capitalization process and market integration have changed ethnic identities and relationships at two levels, with the state and among the villagers themselves. Although these relational shifts have occurred, they have generated socio-economic dynamics in highland communities that may lead to new perspectives.
papers.keywords: Agrarian Capitalism · State Engagement · Zomia · Akha · Coffee

papers.title: When the Highlands Move: Coffee, Akha, Tai Dam, and the Shifting Geography of Belonging in Thailand
papers.abstract: Coffee cultivation in Thailand has transformed from a state-led development strategy associated with ethnic minority incorporation into a commodity through which ethnic and regional identities are produced, negotiated, and represented. This paper examines this transformation through two cases: Akha coffee production in the northern highlands and Tai Dam coffee initiatives in Loei Province, Isan. The first case examines Akha Ama Coffee, tracing how coffee cultivation became embedded in changing relationships among ethnic identity, state development, markets, and representations of the highlands. The second examines institutional operations and the promotion of coffee among Tai Dam communities in Loei, focusing on how coffee has become connected to regional development and the articulation of Tai Dam and Isan identities. Drawing on historical texts, secondary literature, institutional documents, and interviews with three coffee producers, the paper employs Benedict Anderson’s concept of the “imagined community” alongside Bourdieu’s concepts of habitus and hysteresis to examine relationships between ethnicity, place, and structures of power. Moving from ethnic highlands to an ethnic minority community in the Isan lowlands, the paper argues that the “center” of coffee production and identity-making is not fixed. Coffee landscapes reveal how ethnic and regional belonging are reconstructed through state policy, markets, institutions, and agency.
papers.keywords: Isan · Tai Dam · Akha

papers.title: Coffee and Everyday World-Making among Akha in Northern Thailand
papers.abstract:
正文 **285 词**，符合主办方个人／合著论文摘要不超过300词的要求；访谈保留计划时态。[投稿要求](https://rcsd.soc.cmu.ac.th/uncategorized/call-for-abstracts-coffee-landscapes-of-the-southeast-asia-region/)

Marx’s (1859) proposition that “the mode of production of material life conditions the general process of social, political and intellectual life” frames this comparison of Hani rice cultivation in Honghe, Akha tea cultivation in Mengsong, Xishuangbanna, and Akha coffee production in northern Thailand. Drawing on Marx’s (1867) account of reproduction and Althusser’s (1971) analysis of education, the study examines how production relations shape cultural knowledge and identity.

The research is primarily qualitative. Planned interviews with Ardang, Jesada Netawong and members of Seeds Journey will be analysed alongside published ethnographies of Hani and Akha communities, research published by Chiang Mai University’s Regional Center for Social Science and Sustainable Development, and Chinese and Thai policy and development project documents. Comparative analysis will connect interview accounts of livelihood and cultural change with documented shifts in land governance and education.

The analysis approaches cultivation, ritual and learning as interconnected practices. It examines how land regulation, commodity markets and development programmes reorganise crop choices, labour, resource control and the distribution of returns, while schooling and project training reshape skills, aspirations and cultural judgements. These processes alter opportunities to learn ancestral languages, lineage histories and ritual practices, influencing what people regard as backward, useful or worth preserving.

Such changes also inform public cultural expression. Dress, performances and historical narratives can become ways of asserting distinctiveness, national belonging and rights. Cultural recognition, however, need not restore authority over knowledge or resources.

The study traces how these changing understandings subsequently inform cultivation, employment, education and ritual participation, thereby sustaining, revising or contesting production relations. It conceptualises knowledge production as a recurring interaction between material production, learning and subject formation, locating differences between Chinese and Thai trajectories within their specific historical and institutional conditions.
papers.keywords: Coffee · Akha · world-making · knowledge production · social reproduction · northern Thailand.

sessions.name: Producing Coffee Knowledge in Highland Communities

papers.title: Tracing Coffee’s Place in Ethnobotanical Practice: case study from Mae Klang Luang Karen Village, Chiang Mai
papers.abstract: Despite its non-native origins, coffee has established a cultivated relationship with highland ethnic groups in northern Thailand. In Chiang Mai province, the Karen highland ethnic group is widely recognized for their coffee-crafting practices. This paper applies an ethnobotanical lens and discussion to explore how coffee as both a plant and an economic product continuously reshapes social and cultural dynamics in Mae Klang Luang Karen Village. Four decades after its introduction as a substitute to opium through King Rama IX’s Royal Project, coffee has evolved from an unfamiliar cash crop into the village’s signature. Through institutional sharing knowledge from the Royal Project and other institutions, Mae Klang Luang has transformed coffee into a cultural tradition and tourism experience by serving coffee as a welcome drink. This study employs qualitative fieldwork including in-depth and semi-structured interviews as well as participant’s observation. The study finds a threefold impact: ecologically, a shade-grown coffee practice enhances forest conservation, economically, coffee shops serve as the hub for selling local products such as local fruits and vegetables and handicrafts such as hand-woven clothes and bags, and culturally, nature trail tourism led by local Karen guides turn coffee origin stories into immersive ethnobotanical learning for tourists. These findings demonstrate how a single plant species can reshape a community’s development path, highlighting the role of ethnobotanical traditions in contemporary highland livelihoods.
papers.keywords: Ethnobotany · Coffee culture · Karen ethnic group

papers.title: Producing Culture: The Inward Flow of Coffee Knowledge and the Transformation of Everyday and Ritual Practice in Doi Chang, a Coffee-Producing Community in Northern Thailand
papers.abstract: Coffee travels from mountain villages to urban cafés as a tradable commodity, yet the culture that surrounds it moves in the opposite direction—flowing from consumer markets back into the communities where the beans are cultivated. Drawing on ethnographic fieldwork in Doi Chang, a highland ethnic minority village in northern Thailand, this paper examines how coffee culture has flowed back from consumer markets into the place of production since the industry's establishment in the region. The study finds that this inward cultural flow operates on two interconnected levels. First, villagers have acquired practical knowledge of post-harvest processing, roasting, and sensory evaluation through institutional training programs, on-site guidance from external coffee companies, and informal master-apprentice relationships within the village. These newly acquired skills have transformed them from growers who merely sell fresh cherries into practitioners capable of engaging in processing activities such as sorting, grading, and roasting. Second, coffee has entered the everyday social and ritual life of the community. Visiting a neighbor's house to share coffee and conversation has become a regular social practice, while coffee has also been incorporated into local ceremonial contexts, acquiring meanings that extend far beyond its economic value as a cash crop. This bidirectional movement reveals that producing communities are not merely passive starting points for raw materials flowing out along global value chains, but are also active sites where external coffee culture settles, is reabsorbed, and takes on locally specific forms. Consequently, the relationship between villagers and coffee has expanded from a simple grow-and-sell exchange into a complex interweaving of production, processing, tasting, social hospitality, and ritual consumption.
papers.keywords: knowledge flow · occupational change · Thailand coffee · coffee-producing community

papers.title: Seeing Sustainability: A Participatory Visual Study of Coffee Farmers’ Knowledge, Negotiation, and Aspirations
papers.abstract: This paper examines how smallholder coffee farmers in Nan Province, Northern Thailand, produce, negotiate, and transmit knowledge about sustainable farming outside formal institutional channels. Using Photovoice, semi-structured interviews, and a focus group with seven farmers, the study investigates farming as a site of active knowledge production and informal pedagogy, not merely a technical or economic activity. Findings show farmers departing from standardised agricultural guidance in favour of experientially validated adaptations. For example, farmers modified planting techniques after observing that official recommendations reduced seedling survival in dry-season conditions. Such knowledge is generated through trial-and-error, peer exchange, and intergenerational transmission, circulating through informal networks such as farmer messaging groups, mentorship, and school partnerships rather than expert-led instruction. Farmers also position themselves explicitly as educators: training new growers, integrating coffee cultivation into school curricula, and treating farming itself as an experiential pedagogy for younger generations. These practices challenge the assumption, still embedded in agricultural extension and certification systems, that expertise flows primarily from institutions to farmers. By centring farmers' own images and narratives, the study documents them as knowledge holders and co-producers of expertise, whose innovations are frequently unrecognised within formal knowledge hierarchies. The paper contributes to discussions of epistemic justice in agricultural knowledge systems, arguing that participatory visual methods can surface locally legitimate expertise that conventional knowledge-transfer models overlook. It offers implications for how knowledge production in the coffee sector is understood beyond its commercial and technical dimensions to include the informal, experiential systems through which smallholders actually generate, validate, and pass on sustainability knowledge.
papers.keywords: Knowledge Production · Coffee Farming · Thailand · Epistemic Justice · Participatory Visual Methods

papers.title: From Fresh Tea Leaves to Coffee Cherries: Remaking Practices and Knowledge in a Highland Borderland
papers.abstract: Over the past four decades, state-led development and market expansion have changed agricultural practices in the highlands of Northern Thailand. Previous highland agricultural development programs that promoted different crops in different areas, including vegetables, tea, and coffee, contributed to differentiated agricultural landscapes and crop-specific practices and knowledge. However, these agricultural landscapes are not fixed. Growing markets and private actors have increasingly influenced how new crops and practices enter areas with established crop patterns. This paper examines these changes through three neighboring ethnic highland communities in Chiang Rai, which share a similar tea-based agricultural history. While coffee is not new to all of these communities, it is becoming more visible even in areas well known for tea. Coffee has entered these communities through different pathways, which allows me to examine how farmers manage existing and new practices. This paper employs the concept of landscape plasticity to examine how farmers draw on different forms of agricultural and market knowledge as coffee enters existing tea-based landscapes. These practices differ depending on how coffee enters the community and farmers’ access to knowledge, networks and markets. Initial observations from fieldwork on tea production suggest that many farmers continue to rely on tea as a regular source of income, while introducing coffee as an additional crop. Many sell coffee cherries or parchment rather than processing it further, similar to how they sell fresh tea leaves. Others with more financial resources, stronger social networks, and greater market knowledge have more options to experiment with further processing, develop their own brands, explore specialty coffee markets, and continue supplying larger markets. These observations suggest that coffee does not simply replace tea but gradually remakes agricultural practices and knowledge. This process is uneven, showing how landscape plasticity can take different forms within the same highland borderland.
papers.keywords: Chiang Rai · Coffee · Landscape Plasticity · Agricultural Knowledge

blocks.title: Plenary discussion II: Coffee, Land and Forest: Climate and Livelihoods of Upland Growers in Southeast Asia: Cases from Indonesia, Viet Nam, Thailand and Laos PDR
blocks.about: Coffee has been promoted across the uplands of the region as a crop that increases household income while maintaining forest cover. The income gains are documented. The associated costs are less often recorded. This plenary presents four cases. In Manggarai, Indonesia, competing claims between customary cultivation and state-designated protected forest led to violence and a human rights investigation. In Dien Bien, Viet Nam, commercialisation has shifted land, labour and investment away from subsistence production, increasing cash income while raising exposure to price and climate risk. In Thailand, growers cultivate land within a forest zone without formal documentation, which limits what they can plan, sell and transfer. Speakers will discuss what households lose in these transitions and what is required for them to farm securely.
